question: What did Acme Corp say about their current workflow?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract everything the Acme prospect says about their current workflow: how they handle the process today, tools or systems they use, manual steps, bottlenecks, and pain points.
assumptions: 'Acme Corp' is mapped to 'Acme Logistics' (CALL-001), the only catalogue company with an Acme name.
The question refers to a single call, so no call_types restriction is applied.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The short version is we've got too much operational work living between systems.
findings.context: Acme's operational work lives across multiple systems; they already have dashboards but need something that moves work along and shows ownership. — Rachel's opening description of the current state, framing the problem before any product discussion

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders. So renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late.
findings.context: Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success are run through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so renewal risks and implementation blockers are noticed late, sometimes a week late or only at the QBR. — Concrete example of the current manual process and its delay

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something runs, then nothing happens for four days, then a human notices.
findings.context: Acme has some automation, but the failure point is the gaps between automated pieces, where work stalls for days before a human notices. — Rachel corrects the assumption that the process is fully manual

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact.
findings.context: Acme's operational telemetry is weak: they can tell a process was late only after the fact and struggle to explain why, which dependency failed, or how often it recurs. — Rachel on measurement gaps in the current setup

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We have at least two scripts running that I could not tell you the author of.
findings.context: Acme runs unowned scripts: Rachel said at least two, Tom corrected it to three, and nobody can say who wrote them. — Self-correction between the two customers on the count of scripts

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: In practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions.
findings.context: Onboarding is not standardised: EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions, so the documented process differs from the one actually run. — Tom correcting the earlier description of onboarding as standardised

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: a lot of the actual context is in chat, which is — that's the problem, isn't it.
findings.context: Much of the actual process context lives in chat, and the system of record varies by object, so no single system holds the process. — Rachel on where process data sits across the stack

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: The data team uses it for a handful of back-office integrations. It works. But RevOps finds it too technical
findings.context: Acme already uses Workato for a handful of back-office integrations; the data team uses it and it works, but RevOps finds it too technical. — Tom describing the existing iPaaS and its limits for business users

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
findings.context: Integrations have broken silently when source schemas changed, such as renamed fields or new picklist values. — Tom describing a past failure mode of current automation

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context.
findings.context: Acme's expensive staff spend time on coordination work because their systems don't carry enough process context; hidden engineering upkeep on scripts also accumulates over time. — Rachel on the cost of the current approach; Tom on maintenance cost

rejected_findings.claim: Acme already has automation that nobody clearly owns; when something fails, escalation depends on whoever happens to notice it.
rejected_findings.quote: We've already got automation nobody quite owns. When something sticks, the escalation path depends entirely on who happens to see it.
rejected_findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez (customer, Director of Customer Success)
rejected_findings.reason: quote not found in cited turns

draft.answer: Acme Logistics' Rachel Morgan and Tom Alvarez described operational work spread across systems and managed manually through spreadsheets and Slack, with delayed detection of problems [C1][C2]. Automation exists but stalls in the gaps between pieces, and telemetry is weak [C3][C4]. They also cited unowned scripts, inconsistent onboarding, Workato limits, silent integration failures and costly coordination work [C5][C6][C7][C8].

claims.text: Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations) said Acme has too much operational work living between systems; they already have dashboards but need something that moves work along and shows ownership.

Rachel said handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success are managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so renewal risks and implementation blockers are noticed late (sometimes a week late or only at the QBR).
Rachel said Acme has some automation, but the problem is the gaps between automated pieces: something runs, then nothing happens for four days until a human notices.
Rachel said operational telemetry is weak: they can tell something was late only after the fact and struggle to explain why, which dependency failed, or how often it recurs.

Acme runs unowned scripts: Rachel said at least two, Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success) corrected it to three, and nobody can say who wrote them. Rachel also noted hidden engineering upkeep on scripts accumulates.
Tom said onboarding is not standardised: EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions, so the documented process differs from the one actually run.
Rachel said much of the actual process context lives in chat, and the system of record varies by object, so no single system holds the process.
Tom said Acme already uses Workato for a handful of back-office integrations by the data team; it works, but RevOps finds it too technical.
Tom said integrations have died silently when someone renamed a field or added a picklist value.
Rachel said expensive staff spend time on coordination work because systems don't carry enough process context.

conflicts.description: Onboarding was earlier described as standardised, but Tom corrected that EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions in practice.
Rachel said at least two scripts with unknown authors; Tom corrected the count to three.
Rachel corrected the assumption that the process is fully manual: some automation exists, but it fails in the gaps.

assumptions: 'Acme Corp' is mapped to Acme Logistics (CALL-001).
